findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys that evaluate to literal strings, making the schema non-functional
findings.body: The expressions `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` evaluate to the literal strings `"ZodString"` and `"ZodOptional"` respectively, not dynamic key patterns. This means the schema requires a property literally named "ZodString" with a number value, which no real OAuth token response will have. When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is true, `safeParse` will always fail, causing `parseRefreshTokenResponse` to throw "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" for every token refresh, completely breaking the credential sharing feature. The intended behavior was likely `.passthrough()` or `.catchall(z.unknown())`.

findings.title: Inconsistent return type breaks callers when credential sharing is enabled
findings.body: When credential sharing is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw `fetch` `Response` object. When disabled, it returns whatever `refreshFunction()` returns (e.g., a GaxiosResponse with `.data` for Google, a HubspotToken object for Hubspot, an AxiosResponse with `.data` for Zoho). Callers like Google Calendar (`res?.data`), Hubspot (`hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate`), and Zoho Bigin (`tokenInfo.data.error`) will crash or produce undefined values when credential sharing is enabled because a `Response` object doesn't have those properties.

findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported, causing a ReferenceError at runtime
findings.body: The newly added code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` on line 96, but `prisma` is not imported anywhere in this file. The existing imports include jsforce, rrule, zod, and various @calcom packages, but not `@calcom/prisma`. This will throw a ReferenceError the first time the Salesforce calendar service attempts to refresh a token.

findings.title: Placeholder string "refresh_token" stored as actual refresh token value
findings.body: When the parsed token response lacks a `refresh_token` field, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` (a literal placeholder string). This value is then persisted to the database via `prisma.credential.update` in callers like Google Calendar and Office 365. On the next token refresh cycle, this placeholder will be sent to the OAuth provider, which will reject it, permanently breaking the credential until manually fixed.

findings.title: Webhook secret comparison is not timing-safe
findings.body: The webhook secret is compared using `!==` (line 25-27), which is vulnerable to timing attacks. An attacker can iteratively guess the secret character by character by measuring response times. For security-sensitive secret comparisons, `crypto.timingSafeEqual` should be used after ensuring both buffers are the same length.

findings.title: No HTTP method restriction on credential webhook endpoint
findings.body: The handler does not check `req.method`, so it accepts GET, PUT, DELETE, etc. in addition to POST. This increases the attack surface (e.g., secrets could appear in server access logs via GET query parameters if a proxy rewrites headers). The endpoint should restrict to POST only.

findings.title: Credential ID passed where user ID is expected in refreshOAuthTokens call
findings.body: The third argument to `refreshOAuthTokens` is `credentialId` (the credential's database primary key from line 53), but the function's parameter is named `userId` and is sent to the external sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. The external service will receive a credential ID instead of a user ID, making it unable to look up the correct user's tokens. It should be the user's ID associated with the credential.

findings.title: Zod parse throws unhandled error returning 500 instead of 400 for invalid input
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` will throw a `ZodError` if the request body doesn't match the schema. Without a try/catch or `.safeParse()`, this results in an unhandled exception and a 500 Internal Server Error response instead of a proper 400 Bad Request, leaking implementation details in the error response.

findings.title: Hubspot token refresh will crash when credential sharing is enabled due to type mismatch
findings.body: When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is true, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw `fetch` Response object. The code assigns it to `hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken` and immediately accesses `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` (line 192) and `hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken` (line 202), which are properties of the HubSpot SDK's token object, not of a `Response`. This will result in `undefined` values being stored and used, breaking the HubSpot integration.
